testCases.name: test_case_7
testCases.input: what are the different risk categories we evaluate an LLM app on?
testCases.actualOutput: The risk categories for evaluating an LLM application include correctness and accuracy, relevance, completeness, instruction following, safety, and operational aspects. Correctness and accuracy assess whether the generated content is accurate, while relevance checks if the answer relates to the question asked. Completeness ensures all questions receive answers, and instruction following verifies adherence to specified formats or lengths. Safety involves preventing leaks or jailbreaks, and operational factors consider the application's performance in terms of speed, cost, and reliability.
testCases.expectedOutput: There are three risk categories. Quality checks whether the output is good, for example correct, relevant, and grounded. Safety checks whether the output is harmful, for example toxic content, leaking personal information, or being jailbroken. Operations checks the running characteristics of the system such as latency, cost, and token usage. A full eval suite covers all three, not just quality.

testCases.name: test_case_6
testCases.input: why do we need multiple eval pipelines for a single application instead of just one?
testCases.actualOutput: Multiple eval pipelines are needed for a single application because there are multiple failure points and different risk categories. For instance, in a rag chatbot, failures can occur at the component level, workflow level, and application level, necessitating separate eval pipelines to monitor each aspect effectively.
testCases.expectedOutput: Because a single LLM application has multiple failure points and multiple risk categories, so one eval cannot cover it. There are different failure points at the component, workflow, and application levels, and each needs its own eval. There are also different risk categories, quality, safety, and operations, that require different metrics. So you build several eval pipelines and run them together as an eval suite.

testCases.name: test_case_5
testCases.input: what is drift and why does it matter after deployment?
testCases.actualOutput: Drift refers to the gradual obsolescence of the evaluation setup used for a system, which occurs as the system's environment or underlying data changes over time. It matters after deployment because if the evaluation setup does not adapt to these changes, the results from the initial evaluations may no longer be relevant or accurate. For example, if a chart bot's underlying documents or pricing structures change, the performance metrics that were once valid may no longer reflect the current state of the system, leading to potential issues in its effectiveness.
testCases.expectedOutput: Drift is the gradual degradation of a deployed system's performance over time as real-world data or usage patterns move away from what the system was built and evaluated on. Users may start asking new kinds of questions or the knowledge base may go stale, so metrics slowly fall even though the code did not change. It matters because these failures appear silently in production, so you monitor metrics over time, set alerts when they drop, and feed failing cases back into your offline dataset.

testCases.name: test_case_4
testCases.input: offline eval vs online eval - what's the difference?
testCases.actualOutput: The difference between offline eval and online eval lies in their purposes and contexts. Offline eval checks if an application is working correctly before deployment, using a fixed dataset, while online eval determines if the application is running normally in production, working with live traffic and without a predefined answer key. Offline eval is fast, cheap, and repeatable, whereas online eval can be costly due to the need to monitor many conversations in real-time. Both evaluations are complementary and serve different roles in the evaluation process.
testCases.expectedOutput: Offline eval happens before deployment on a fixed golden dataset in a controlled setting; it is usually reference-based and is what you run during development to decide whether a version is good enough to ship. Online eval happens after deployment on live production traffic, works without ground-truth labels, and relies on real user interactions and signals like thumbs up/down, latency, and cost. Offline gates deployment; online monitors real behaviour.

testCases.name: test_case_8
testCases.input: as an AI engineer why do I even need model evals?
testCases.actualOutput: As an AI engineer, model evaluations are important because they provide mechanisms to measure the capabilities of different LLMs, which is essential for making informed decisions about which models to use in your applications. Without model evaluations, you would lack the necessary insights to compare models effectively, making it difficult to choose the right one for your projects. For instance, when deciding between using a proprietary LLM or an open-source model, model evaluations help you understand the strengths and weaknesses of each option.
testCases.expectedOutput: Because you have to choose which model to use for your application, and model evals give you a concrete, measurable basis for that decision rather than guessing. Benchmarks let you compare general capabilities of models, and when you need to know which model is best for your specific task you run custom model evals on your own data. Without model evals you cannot justify model selection objectively.

testCases.name: test_case_3
testCases.input: what does reference-based vs reference-free eval mean?
testCases.actualOutput: Reference-based evaluation involves having a known correct answer or answer key for each test case, allowing the evaluation to be done by comparing the output against this reference. In contrast, reference-free evaluation does not have a predefined correct answer; instead, it relies on human judgment and a rubric to assess the quality of the output.
testCases.expectedOutput: A reference-based eval needs a ground-truth answer to compare against, a golden or expected output authored ahead of time, and scores the system by how close it comes to that reference. A reference-free eval needs no ground truth and instead judges an intrinsic property of the output, usually with an LLM as a judge. The test is simply whether the metric requires an expected answer.

testCases.name: test_case_12
testCases.input: what is pass@1 and how is it different from pass@k?
testCases.actualOutput: Pass@1 involves asking a model a single question and determining if the answer it provides is correct or not. In contrast, pass@k, such as pass@5, requires asking the same question multiple times (in this case, five) and considering the model to have provided a correct answer if it answers correctly at least once out of those attempts. Thus, pass@k is a more lenient evaluation strategy compared to pass@1.
testCases.expectedOutput: Pass@1 means the model is given one attempt at a question and is scored on whether that single answer is correct; it is the standard setting, usually run with temperature 0. Pass@k means the model is allowed k attempts and is counted as passing if at least one of the k attempts is correct. Pass@k is more lenient than pass@1 because more attempts raise the chance of getting at least one right.

testCases.name: test_case_2
testCases.input: what are the different methods to actually perform an eval?
testCases.actualOutput: There are three methods to perform an evaluation: programmatic methods, LLMEval-based methods using a judge, and evaluations conducted with humans. Each of these methods can be used to assess the output of LLMs or LLM-powered applications.
testCases.expectedOutput: There are three broad methods. Programmatic (deterministic) evaluation uses code and fixed rules to check the output, which is cheap and reliable but only works when correctness can be expressed in code. LLM-as-a-judge uses a capable LLM to score outputs, which handles subjective or semantic judgments at scale. Human evaluation uses people to judge outputs, which is the most reliable for nuanced quality but the slowest and most expensive.

testCases.name: test_case_9
testCases.input: what is a benchmark and what does MMLU test?
testCases.actualOutput: A benchmark is a standardized test used to measure a specific model capability, consisting of four main components: a data set or task, run configuration, scoring method, and aggregation method. MMLU tests model intelligence and knowledge by using existing exams to evaluate how well models can perform on these assessments.
testCases.expectedOutput: A benchmark is a standardized model eval: a fixed dataset and scoring procedure used to compare the capabilities of different models on the same footing. MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) is a multiple-choice benchmark covering many subjects that measures the breadth of a model's knowledge. It does not measure reasoning depth, calibration, open-ended generation, and it is English and exam-style only.
